item.title: Why I love Madrid in winter: ‘Locals get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: engaging narrative, cultural insight, and vivid description

Live in Madrid long enough and you hear the same weather-related proverbs again and again. One old saying goes that the seasons in the Spanish capital break down to “nine months of winter and three months of hell”. And if the city never quite freezes over in the coldest months – except for the blizzard of the century that came with Storm Filomena in 2021 – it is also said that the subtle, evil wind coming in from the mountains could kill a person without snuffing a candle.

Personally, I prefer it here at this time of year, though if you’re looking to escape the crowds you might be disappointed. Madrid has only got busier in the 11 years I’ve lived here, and Christmas feels more crowded than midsummer on the central streets around Puerta del Sol. All the main public squares get their own giant Christmas trees, while Plaza de España and Plaza Colón install ice rinks too, and a festive market fills the cobbled core of Plaza Mayor with painted wooden huts. Many local people get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats, and one of my seasonal highlights is spotting couples or whole families engaged in furious arguments while wearing reindeer antlers or giant turkeys on their heads.

It’s nice to see the Christmas lights up close, especially where they’re themed and art-directed by guest designers across the facade of the Four Seasons hotel and the flagship store of Spanish leatherware brand Loewe. But it’s often better to get a little distance, and El Cielo de Montera is my favourite of the city’s competing roof terraces. With the Gran Vía below and the glowing blue art deco clock of the Telefónica building above, winter in Madrid looks a little like 1930s Manhattan from this angle.

Civic life continues outdoors, and there’s great sensory pleasure to dining in the cold air under lap blankets and patio heaters, though I also love the huddled feel of retreating deep inside a vintage tavern. Mulled wine isn’t a big thing in Spain but they do a good one at Vinícola Mentridana, an atmospheric bodega, and if you think of sherry as a winter drink, at the beautifully basic La Venencia it’s the only thing that has been served since 1922. There are five varieties poured straight from the casks.

For something truly warming, cocido madrileño is this region’s signature stew of chickpeas, noodles, cabbage and pork meats, rationed out in three courses, or vuelcos, of such absurd abundance at Malacatín that fourth-generation owner Jose Rodríguez says only three diners have ever completed the full meal in the century-plus his family has run the place.

Most winters, the only snow to be seen is in paintings such as Goya’s La Nevada at the Prado, which is best enjoyed in the relative quiet of lunchtimes during mid-November or mid-January, when the city empties a bit. Some flakes will likely fall across the Sierra de Guadarrama though, where King Felipe II built El Escorial circa 1580. Above that palace and monastery, forest trails lead to mountain lookouts. Seen from there, a distance of about 30 miles (50km), faraway Madrid becomes a winter mirage – sharp and glinting under crystal-blue skies, a futuristic vision seen from a now-remote past.

Where to stay

7 Islas (doubles from €113) in the city centre has light, airy rooms and a designer lobby with an art gallery and craft cocktail bar.

Source: The Guardian Travel | Published: 2026-11-22 07:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: A guide to lounge access with the Amex Platinum and Business Platinum
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful information for frequent travelers, but lacks depth in learning value

Editorial note: This is a recurring post, regularly updated with new information and offers.

- Premium travel cards can provide access to a wide range of airport lounges worldwide, including Centurion, Delta Sky Club, Priority Pass, Escape, Plaza Premium and other partner lounges.

- Lounge entry policies, guest access and amenities vary by network and location, with some lounges offering complimentary food, drinks and unique features like family rooms or table service.

- Guest access at Centurion Lounges in the U.S. typically requires a fee unless a significant annual spending threshold is met, which unlocks complimentary guest privileges for a set period.

- Access to Delta Sky Clubs is limited to a set number of annual visits unless a high spending requirement is achieved, and guest entry is available for a fee.

What to consider

- Lounge access requires presenting your eligible card, government-issued identification and a same-day boarding pass; some networks require separate enrollment.

- Entry windows are enforced, such as the three-hour rule before departure for Centurion Lounges and similar timing for Delta Sky Clubs; arrival access is generally not permitted except during layovers.

- Guest policies and fees differ by lounge network and may change based on annual spending or specific lounge rules.

What you'll miss from the article

- A detailed breakdown of lounge networks, access requirements, guest policies and tips for maximizing your airport lounge experience.
